opus-5.5.text:
I think one of the things people underappreciate is that the speed changes not just *what* decisions get made, but *how* they get made, and often in ways that aren't great.

When a technology moves on a timescale of decades, institutions have time to absorb it. You get hearings, you get studies, you get a generation of people who grow up with it and develop intuitions. With AI, the capability curve is moving on a timescale of months. So what happens in practice is that a lot of really consequential decisions end up being made by a relatively small number of people, under time pressure, with incomplete information. And I include myself in that. I don't think that's a good state of affairs. It's just the state of affairs we're in.

There's a kind of compression that happens. If you're running a company at the frontier, you're making calls about what to train, what to release, what safeguards are sufficient, and the next model is already in the pipeline before you've fully understood the last one. Government is in an even harder position, because its natural cadence is slower. By the time a policy process concludes, the thing it was designed around may look quaint.

So I think about this in a few ways. One is that you want to build mechanisms that can move at the speed of the technology. Things like responsible scaling policies are partly an attempt at that. You commit in advance: if a model crosses certain capability thresholds, these are the things we'll do. That way you're not relitigating everything from scratch under pressure. You've made the decision in a calmer moment, when you could think clearly.

The second is transparency. If decisions are going to be made quickly, at least they should be legible. Other people, governments, researchers, the public, should be able to see what's happening and push back. Speed plus opacity is the really dangerous combination.

And the third, honestly, is a kind of humility. When things are moving this fast, your confidence in any particular forecast should be lower than it feels. I've been surprised in both directions. So you want to make decisions that are robust, that preserve options, that don't lock you into a path you can't get off if you turn out to be wrong.

The thing I worry about most is that competitive pressure turns speed into an excuse. "We have to move fast because the other guy is moving fast." There's some truth in that, which is exactly what makes it dangerous. I think the job is to hold both things at once: take the race dynamics seriously, but don't let them become a reason to stop thinking carefully.

r001.rationale: It says many consequential decisions are made under time pressure, with the next model already in the pipeline before the last is fully understood, conveying that rapid development crowds out deliberation.

r002.rationale: The response mentions incomplete information and uncertainty about forecasts, but does not say decision-makers may not know which decisions will later prove consequential.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the things I worry about most, and it's maybe underappreciated relative to the more dramatic risks people talk about.

The basic problem is that the pace of the technology is just much faster than the pace at which institutions make decisions. If you look at how a government or a large company or even a lab like ours makes a genuinely consequential decision, there's a process. People gather information, they deliberate, there are checks, there's some kind of accountability. That process has a certain natural timescale, usually months or years. And the technology is moving on a timescale of months, sometimes weeks. So you end up with this mismatch where the decisions that matter most are being made under enormous time pressure, often by a small number of people, with much less information than you'd want.

And I'd say there are a couple of ways this plays out. One is that decisions get made by default. Nobody actually decides, the thing just happens because the train is moving and no one stopped it. I think a lot of what's happened in the last few years looks like that. The second is that when someone does decide, they're deciding in a competitive environment. If we don't do it, someone else will. That's often true, which is uncomfortable, but it also means the decision is really being made by the structure of the race rather than by anyone's judgment about what's good.

What I try to do about this, and I'm not claiming we get it right, is to front-load the thinking. If you can't deliberate carefully in the moment, you deliberate ahead of time. That's basically the logic of something like a responsible scaling policy. You say, in advance, here are the capabilities that would worry us, here's what we'd need to have in place before we proceed, and you commit to that when you're calm and not under pressure. Then when the moment comes, you're executing a decision rather than making one from scratch at two in the morning.

The other thing is that I think the speed actually argues for being more conservative about certain things, not less. There's a view that says, because things are moving fast, we have to move fast too, we can't afford to be careful. And there's some truth to that in the competitive sense. But the faster things move, the less you can rely on being able to course-correct later. Mistakes compound. So the cost of getting an irreversible decision wrong goes up, and that should make you want more margin, not less.

I'll also say the honest version of this, which is that the people in my position have more power over these decisions than I think anyone should have. I don't think that's a stable or healthy situation. Part of why I talk publicly about this stuff, and part of why I think policy matters even when it's clumsy, is that the goal should be to get these decisions out of the hands of a few labs and into something more legitimate, before the window for doing that closes. And the speed of development is exactly what makes that window short.

r001.rationale: The response says AI moves faster than institutional decision processes, leaving consequential decisions under time pressure and with less information. It does not explain that a volume of simultaneous decisions limits deliberation on each one.

r002.rationale: The response discusses decisions that matter most but does not state that decision-makers may not know which decisions will later prove consequential.

astra-6.text:
I think the speed makes it much harder to separate understanding what’s happening from deciding what to do about it. Normally, you’d hope to have a period where the technology develops, people study its implications, institutions build expertise, and then consequential decisions get made. With AI, those things may have to happen almost simultaneously.

Imagine a model suddenly becomes much better at some class of scientific tasks. You have to figure out how real that capability is, what benefits it could produce, whether it creates new risks, and what deployment should look like. And while you’re doing that, you’re training the next model. The object you’re trying to understand is changing underneath you.

That puts a lot of weight on decisions made before the moment of pressure. What evidence would cause us to slow down? What tests do we need to run? Who has the authority to say that something isn’t ready? If you leave all of that until you have an exciting new system and enormous pressure to release it, you’ve made the decision harder than it needs to be.

The other thing is that speed can concentrate decision-making among the few people who have the most current information. That’s a problem, because having the best technical information doesn’t necessarily give you the legitimacy to make decisions that affect everyone. So part of the challenge is getting outside institutions enough visibility and expertise that they can participate meaningfully, even as the technology moves quickly.

r001.rationale: The response says AI development forces understanding and decisions to happen almost simultaneously, but does not state that the volume of decisions limits deliberation on each one.

r002.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about capabilities, benefits, and risks, but does not say decision-makers may not know which decisions will prove consequential when they make them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the speed creates this tension where the decisions are becoming more consequential at the same time that the window for making them is getting shorter. Normally, when a technology changes society, you have some time to understand what’s happening, build institutions around it, and correct mistakes. With AI, you may be making a decision about the next system while you’re still trying to understand the effects of the last one.

And that means a lot ends up depending on a relatively small number of people who happen to be in the room. I find that concerning even when those people are thoughtful and well-intentioned. Their judgment matters, but it shouldn’t be the entire mechanism by which society makes these choices.

So the thing I’d emphasize is doing as much of the thinking as possible in advance. What capabilities would make us worried? What evidence would cause us to delay a release? Who needs to be involved in that decision? You want to establish those processes before there’s an immediate commercial incentive to explain away a troubling result.

Of course, you can’t anticipate everything. You need to learn from the systems themselves. But speed makes preparation more valuable, because when the consequential moment arrives, you may have very little time to invent a good decision-making process.

r001.rationale: The response says the window for decisions is shorter and there may be little time to create a process, but it does not state that many decisions arise simultaneously or that their volume limits deliberation on each one.

r002.rationale: The response notes that not everything can be anticipated, but it does not say decision-makers may not know which decisions will later prove consequential.
